2. She showed remarkable tenacity, refusing to give up even after losing the first two sets. --- TENACITY (n) = sự kiên trì, bền bỉ; collocation "sheer/mental tenacity", "show great tenacity"; không nhầm với "tension".
3. Nobody expected the underdog to win the league, but the newly promoted club did. --- UNDERDOG (n) = kẻ yếu thế, bị đánh giá thấp; luôn là danh từ, không dùng như tính từ mô tả trận đấu.
4. The defending champion was a formidable opponent in the final. --- FORMIDABLE (adj) = đáng gờm; collocation "a formidable opponent/team"; trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết đầu.
5. Signing with a major club can be an extremely lucrative move for a young player. --- LUCRATIVE (adj) = sinh lời; collocation "a lucrative deal/contract"; không nhầm với "luxurious".
6. Professional gamers need immense agility, both physical and mental, to compete at the top level. --- AGILITY (n) = sự nhanh nhẹn, linh hoạt; danh từ không đếm được; tính từ tương ứng là "agile".

7. Some critics argue that modern sport increasingly reflects the commodification of athletes, treating them as products to be bought and sold. --- COMMODIFICATION (n) = sự thương mại hoá; collocation "the commodification of sport/talent"; động từ là "commodify".

8. Local clubs and grassroots coaching programmes are essential for discovering new talent at the earliest level. --- GRASSROOTS (adj) = ở cấp cơ sở; luôn viết liền, đứng trước danh từ, ví dụ "grassroots sport/level".

10. Strict doping controls exist to ensure a level playing field for every competitor. --- LEVEL PLAYING FIELD (idiom) = sân chơi công bằng; cụm cố định số ít, dùng với "ensure/create a level playing field".
11. The captain, not the coach, is really the one who calls the shots during the match. --- CALL THE SHOTS (idiom) = người ra quyết định, nắm quyền chỉ đạo; luôn dùng số nhiều "shots".

1. Band 7: Playing team sports helps people develop camaraderie and mutual trust with their teammates.
Band 8: Beyond the physical benefits, team sport cultivates a genuine camaraderie among players, forging bonds of trust that often extend well beyond the pitch.
2. Band 7: Athletes who commit to rigorous training regimes tend to see a marked improvement in their performance over time.
Band 8: Sustained improvement in athletic performance is rarely accidental; it is the product of tenacity and a meticulously structured training regime sustained over months, if not years.
3. Band 7: Suffering defeat can, perhaps counter-intuitively, be an invaluable experience for young competitors.
Band 8: Far from being purely detrimental, defeat often proves instructive for young competitors, exposing weaknesses that victory would otherwise have concealed.
4. Band 7: Many people feel that the sums earned by professional athletes are simply disproportionate to their contribution to society.
Band 8: Whether the astronomical wages commanded by elite athletes are justified remains contentious, given the fleeting nature of most professional careers.
5. Band 7: Doping scandals can severely damage a sport's reputation and undermine public confidence in its fairness.
Band 8: Few things erode public trust in a sport as swiftly as a doping scandal, which calls into question not merely one result but the legitimacy of the level playing field itself.
6. Band 7: Amateur and professional sport are held to markedly different standards, both in terms of resources and expectations.
Band 8: The chasm between amateur and professional sport extends well beyond funding, encompassing divergent expectations around commitment, exposure, and the sheer commodification of talent.
7. Band 7: Taking part in regular competitive sport can bring substantial benefits to both physical and mental wellbeing.
Band 8: Regular engagement in competitive sport confers benefits that extend well beyond physical fitness, fostering resilience, camaraderie, and a durable sense of mental wellbeing.
8. Band 7: A strong sense of sportsmanship is arguably just as important as securing victory itself.
Band 8: Genuine sportsmanship — the grace to win humbly and lose without rancour — arguably matters more in the long run than the outcome of any single contest.

passages.text: The image of elite distance runners jogging along narrow tracks in the Kenyan highlands or the Colorado mountains is familiar from countless documentaries. The assumption behind the practice — that training at altitude produces a measurable advantage when athletes return to sea level — has acquired the status of conventional wisdom in endurance sport. What is less widely appreciated is how recently the underlying physiology has been understood, and how unsettled some of its central questions remain. Two decades of carefully designed studies have shown that the response to thin air is more variable, and the trade-offs more delicate, than coaches once supposed.
passages.title: Thin Air, Heavy Training

passages.text: The dominant framework for altitude training was articulated in the late 1990s by Professor Benjamin Levine, an exercise physiologist now at the University of Texas Southwestern. Levine and his collaborators proposed what they called the live-high, train-low model: athletes sleep at altitudes of around 2,500 metres, where reduced oxygen availability stimulates the kidneys to release a hormone called erythropoietin, which in turn promotes the production of additional red blood cells. They descend each day to lower elevations to train at full intensity, since work at altitude is necessarily slower and may erode finely tuned race pace. The model, refined through a sequence of controlled trials involving collegiate runners, became the basis for many national federation programmes during the 2000s.
passages.title: Thin Air, Heavy Training

passages.text: More recent research, however, has complicated this clean account. Professor Carsten Lundby of the University of Innsbruck has argued for some years that the haematological gains from typical altitude camps are smaller and less consistent than the original studies implied. In a 2018 review of forty-five trials, Lundby's group reported that fewer than half of participants showed a meaningful increase in red cell mass, and that genetic differences in oxygen sensing may account for much of the variation. Some athletes, in his data, gained almost nothing from three weeks at altitude; a smaller subgroup gained considerably. Lundby does not dismiss altitude training, but he insists that uniform federation policies, in which entire squads are sent to camps regardless of individual response, are difficult to justify on present evidence.
passages.title: Thin Air, Heavy Training

passages.text: A second strand of research has examined what happens not in the blood but in the immune system. The American physiologist Professor David Nieman, working with marathon runners since the 1980s, was among the first to document what is now widely called the open-window effect: in the hours after very prolonged or very intense exercise, several measures of immune function appear suppressed, and self-reported rates of upper respiratory infection rise. Combine this pattern with the additional physiological stress of altitude, Nieman has suggested, and athletes may face a brief window during which they are unusually vulnerable to common viruses. Coaches who push athletes through hard sessions at the end of a high-altitude block, he warns, may inadvertently undermine the very preparation they intend to enhance.
passages.title: Thin Air, Heavy Training

passages.text: The open-window thesis has not gone unchallenged. Professor Michael Gleeson of Loughborough University, although a long-standing collaborator with Nieman in some respects, has produced data suggesting that the observed dip in immune markers may not translate cleanly into more frequent infection. Many of the older studies, he argues, relied on athletes' own reports of cold-like symptoms, which can be triggered by airway irritation from cold or dry air rather than by genuine viral illness. When laboratory confirmation is required, the apparent excess of infections among hard-training athletes shrinks substantially. Gleeson agrees that recovery practices matter, but he urges caution against framing every training-induced sniffle as a sign of immune collapse.
passages.title: Thin Air, Heavy Training

passages.text: What appears to be emerging from these debates is a more individualised picture of endurance preparation. Several federations now screen athletes for their haematological response after a first altitude block before committing to repeated camps, and some have begun to monitor markers such as salivary immunoglobulin A — an antibody whose decline has been linked, though not without controversy, to subsequent illness. Sleep, nutrition timing and the careful spacing of hard sessions have moved from the periphery of the discussion to its centre. Coaches who once relied on uniform mileage targets are increasingly being asked to defend their decisions in light of measurable biological feedback from each athlete in their charge. The unspoken assumption that more training, at higher altitudes, with shorter recovery, will reliably produce faster athletes has given way to a more cautious view of dose and response.
passages.title: Thin Air, Heavy Training

passages.text: What no responsible specialist now claims is that altitude training is a guaranteed performance lever, or that the immune costs of heavy endurance work are negligible. The honest position, supported by Levine, Lundby, Nieman and Gleeson alike despite their differences, is that altitude exposure offers a meaningful but variable benefit, that the immune system imposes real limits on the intensity that can be sustained week after week, and that intelligent scheduling matters at least as much as raw mileage. The science of thin-air training, in other words, has become less a matter of universal prescriptions and more a question of attentive individual management.

audio_scripts.text: Right, settle in. Today's tutorial — we're, um, hearing from Mateus and Aisha on sports-physiology research methodology. Mateus, you wanna kick us off? And for the recording, could you spell your surname for me?

Yeah, sure. So I'm Mateus Carvalho — that's C-A-R-V-A-L-H-O, the L-H together sounds like the English "lly". My project was a longitudinal study tracking thirty-six club-level marathon runners across the Highgate Athletic region. (Q1)

Erm, the pilot ran in 2020 — sorry, no, 2019 — and the main wave concluded in 2023. So four years end to end. Originally we'd planned to wrap up in 2022, but the cancellation of three major events, you know, pushed everything back by twelve months. (Q2)
Okay. Tense-wise, just to clarify for the recording — your data collection FINISHED in 2023, you're publishing this year, correct?
Right. Published 2026, but the follow-up cohort we're gonna run starts in 2028.

Well, the dominant theoretical lens here is what Pavel Kolesnikov called the "training-load asymmetry framework". And just to flag the terminology — you'll see related labels in the older literature: overtraining syndrome, workload imbalance, training stress index. All those describe the same construct, more or less. The current scholarly term, though, is training-load asymmetry. I'll stick with that. (Q3)

Yeah, and I'm gonna echo Mateus's framing. In my sample — twenty-eight club-level cyclists across the Riverside cycling clubs — most of the cyclists reported pushing their weekly load INTO the high-risk band at least once a fortnight. Actually, sorry, let me be precise — twenty-one out of twenty-eight, so roughly seventy-five per cent. Only a few — about eleven per cent — never crossed into the high-risk band, and some — fourteen per cent — did it sporadically. (Q4)
Right. Now, Mateus, did your sample confirm the "more-mileage-equals-better-performance" thesis?

Sorta, yeah, but with caveats. Most of the runners I observed did NOT regard raw weekly mileage as the primary predictor of race-day performance. The implicit training contract, well, has shifted. Today's club-level runners see polarised intensity distribution as more important than total volume. Only a small minority — fewer than thirteen per cent — described volume as the dominant variable. (Q5)

And, dunno about you, but I found something interesting on the recovery-monitoring axis. So-called heart-rate-variability-led recovery — where athletes adjust each day's training based on overnight HRV — that's actually accelerating sharply in higher-tier amateur clubs. And the literature suggests this constrains an athlete's tendency to overshoot the high-risk load band.
Hmm. Mateus, did you control for training-history stratum?
Kinda. We stratified by years of structured training. Counter-intuitively, the LEAST experienced quartile reported the highest weekly mileage, not the most experienced.
Well, it's about plan-design naivety — newer runners interpret "more is better" more literally, so they overload.

And one final thing — peer-comparison data. In smaller training groups of three to five athletes, peer-driven workload escalation was, um, considerably steeper than in groups of ten-plus athletes. Researchers attribute it to closer interpersonal visibility of mileage logs.

Right. Now, going back to what Mateus mentioned at the start — that "current scholarly term" — that's the construct we'll operationalise next week. Oh, and Aisha, on your seventy-five-per-cent figure: the implication that cyclists routinely overshoot aligns with Kolesnikov, but Mateus's intensity-distribution finding qualifies it. Good tension. Thanks both. (Q6)

blocks.text: The line graph compares participation rates in four sports — football, swimming, cycling and yoga — among UK adults over a thirty-year span from 1990 to 2020.

Overall, two contrasting trends are evident: traditional sports such as football and swimming experienced a steady decline, whereas cycling and especially yoga witnessed sustained growth. By the end of the period, the historically dominant activities had been overtaken by these newer pursuits, and all four lines converged within a narrow band.

In 1990, swimming was by far the most popular activity at 22%, followed by football at 14%; cycling and yoga remained marginal, at 6% and just 1% respectively. Over the following decades, swimming and football slipped to 11% and 10% by 2020, with football briefly peaking at 16% in 2000 before falling away.

Conversely, cycling rose steadily from 6% to 15%, overtaking football around 2010. Yoga underwent the most dramatic expansion of all, climbing fourteenfold to finish level with cycling at 14%. As a result, by the end of the period the four sports were separated by only five percentage points.
The line graph traces participation rates in four sports — football, swimming, cycling and yoga — among UK adults at decade intervals between 1990 and 2020.

Overall, a clear reversal of fortunes is apparent: the once-dominant traditional sports drifted downwards, while the formerly marginal activities climbed sharply, so that the four lines converged by the close of the period. What had begun as a wide spread of popularity ended in near parity.

In 1990, swimming led comfortably at 22%, with football a distant second at 14%, whereas cycling and yoga languished at 6% and a mere 1%. Thereafter both established sports lost ground: swimming contracted year on year to 11%, while football, having peaked at 16% in 2000, slipped to 10% by 2020.

The emerging pursuits told the opposite story. Cycling advanced steadily upwards to reach 15%, overtaking football at around 2010, while yoga surged fourteenfold to 14%. Strikingly, yoga's gain of thirteen percentage points almost exactly mirrored swimming's loss of eleven, as though one sport's following had migrated wholesale to the other.

blocks.text: Regular participation in competitive sport builds not only physical stamina but also the kind of mental resilience that transfers directly into academic and professional life.
Team sports uniquely inculcate camaraderie, teaching young people to trust teammates and subordinate individual glory to a shared goal.
Grassroots sport gives children from disadvantaged backgrounds a rare level playing field on which talent, rather than family wealth, determines success.
Overcoming adversity on the pitch — a missed penalty, a lost final — often instils a tenacity that athletes later draw on when facing setbacks in ordinary life.
The relentless pursuit of victory can tip into overtraining, leaving young athletes with chronic injuries that shorten what should be a promising career.
Excessive commercialisation of professional leagues has arguably eroded the amateur spirit that once defined grassroots competition.
The pressure to succeed can drive some competitors towards doping, undermining the very fairness that sport is meant to embody.
Obsessive focus on a single sport from an early age can crowd out academic study, leaving athletes ill-prepared for life once their lucrative careers inevitably end.
Astronomical broadcasting deals and sponsorship contracts have turned elite sport into a lucrative global industry, changing why many young people take it up in the first place.
The universal human instinct to test oneself against an opponent explains why competitive sport has thrived in virtually every culture throughout history.
Government investment in grassroots facilities is often driven by a desire to combat rising rates of obesity and a sedentary lifestyle among youth.
The rise of social media has fuelled the commodification of individual athletes, as personal brands now generate as much revenue as performance itself.
Hosting a major tournament can leave a host city with a lasting legacy of upgraded infrastructure, though this benefit is not always evenly distributed.
A doping scandal involving a national team can inflict lasting reputational damage that outlives the athletes' careers by decades.
Widespread commercialisation has concentrated wealth among a handful of elite clubs, eroding level playing field conditions across an entire league.
Sustained perseverance through years of grassroots training frequently produces athletes with the psychological toughness to call the shots under pressure at the highest level.
Governing bodies continually struggle to detect increasingly sophisticated methods of doping, a persistent challenge that undermines public trust in record-breaking performances.
Reconciling the short, physically punishing careers of professional athletes with fair long-term financial planning remains a genuine dilemma for players' unions.
Ensuring that sponsorship revenue reaches grassroots clubs, rather than being hoarded by already formidable franchises, is an unresolved structural problem.
Balancing the competitive intensity required to win with the athlete welfare needed to prevent overtraining continues to divide coaches and sports scientists.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: Independent, well-funded anti-doping agencies with the power to conduct unannounced testing would help restore confidence in fair competition.
Redistributing a fixed share of broadcasting revenue toward grassroots programmes could level the playing field between wealthy and struggling clubs.
Mandatory rest periods and evidence-based periodisation schedules can protect young athletes from career-ending overtraining.
Financial literacy programmes for professional athletes would help many avoid poverty once their brief, lucrative careers come to an end.
Many fans firmly believe that the commercialisation of sport has fundamentally compromised its original spirit of pure competition.
Others argue that sponsorship and lucrative broadcasting deals have simply made high-quality sport accessible to a far wider global audience than ever before.
There is widespread agreement that an underdog story, however rare, remains one of the most emotionally compelling narratives in modern sport.
Some maintain that performance-enhancing drugs should never be tolerated under any circumstances, regardless of how marginal the competitive advantage might be.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: International governing bodies bear primary responsibility for enforcing doping regulations consistently, rather than applying them selectively to less formidable nations.
Coaches have a duty of care to prioritise an athlete's long-term health over the short-term temptation to move the goalposts on training intensity.
National governments must ensure that public funding for grassroots facilities does not evaporate once a global tournament ends.
Parents and youth coaches share responsibility for fostering camaraderie and resilience rather than an unhealthy, results-obsessed mentality in child athletes.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: While critics claim commercialisation has ruined sport, it could equally be argued that sponsorship revenue has funded facilities that grassroots clubs could never otherwise afford.
Although some see astronomical salaries as unjustified, defenders point out that a professional athlete's earning window is exceptionally short and physically punishing.
It is sometimes argued that strict anti-doping rules unfairly penalise athletes for accidental contamination, though regulators counter that due process already accounts for such cases.
Sceptics who dismiss underdog victories as mere statistical outliers overlook the genuine tactical tenacity that often underpins these unlikely triumphs.
As e-sports continue to gain significant traction, traditional definitions of what constitutes legitimate competitive sport are likely to be challenged.
Advances in biometric monitoring may soon allow coaches to detect overtraining before it causes irreversible injury, rather than after the damage is done.
Growing public scrutiny of doping is likely to push governing bodies toward more transparent, athlete-led testing protocols.
Wearable technology and predictive analytics could gradually eclipse traditional scouting methods, reshaping how grassroots talent is identified.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas amateur sport a century ago relied almost entirely on grassroots volunteers, today's elite leagues are driven by sponsorship deals worth billions.
Compared with individual sports, team sports arguably cultivate a deeper sense of camaraderie, since success depends on collective rather than solitary effort.
Unlike the formidable financial resources of top clubs, grassroots organisations frequently operate on razor-thin budgets with minimal sponsorship.
In contrast to the amateur ideal of earlier eras, modern professional sport is now inseparable from its commercialisation and global broadcasting reach.
A well-documented underdog narrative, such as a modestly funded club defeating a formidable, star-studded opponent, illustrates how tenacity can outweigh raw resources.
Longitudinal studies tracking young athletes show a clear correlation between excessive early specialisation and overtraining-related injuries later in their careers.
National anti-doping agency reports provide statistical evidence of how testing technology has evolved to catch increasingly sophisticated methods of cheating.
A personal anecdote about a local grassroots team overcoming limited funding through sheer perseverance can effectively illustrate the argument in a Task 2 essay.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: It is often claimed that the relentless commercialisation of elite professional sport has stripped it of its cultural meaning. While I partly accept this argument, I believe the cultural core of sport remains largely intact.

Those who agree with the commercialisation critique tend to focus on the influence of money at the top level. What now drives many leagues is broadcasting revenue rather than community loyalty: ticket prices in the English Premier League, for example, have risen sharply, pricing ordinary supporters out of stadiums. Governance scandals at FIFA and the IOC have further damaged public trust, and sponsorship contracts sometimes appear to outweigh sporting integrity. From this perspective, sport looks increasingly like an entertainment commodity.

On the other hand, however lucrative modern sport has become, it continues to inspire fans in ways few other cultural products can. Major tournaments routinely unite entire nations behind a shared narrative, and underdog stories — a small club overcoming a far stronger opponent, as Leicester City did in 2016 — still produce moments of genuine camaraderie. Fan-engagement studies suggest that emotional attachment to clubs is deepening rather than weakening in the digital era, which implies that cultural value has been reshaped rather than erased.

In my view, the truth lies between the two positions. Commercialisation has undeniably distorted parts of elite sport, particularly competitive balance and accessibility, but its communal and aspirational dimensions endure. If broadcasting revenue were redistributed more fairly to grassroots clubs, the cultural value of sport could in fact be reinforced rather than diminished.

To conclude, I partly agree that commercialisation has eroded certain traditional aspects of elite sport, yet I do not believe its cultural significance has been lost. Better governance, not nostalgia, is the appropriate response.

Few claims provoke as much debate among sports commentators as the charge that elite professional sport has, through relentless commercialisation, lost its cultural value. While the critique captures real distortions, I only partly agree: the financialisation of sport has reshaped, rather than dismantled, its cultural significance.

There is, admittedly, considerable substance to the commercialisation critique. So heavily are top leagues now dependent on broadcasting rights and corporate sponsorship that the locus of decision-making has shifted from clubs to media conglomerates. Governance scandals at FIFA and the IOC have eroded public trust, while ticket-price inflation in competitions such as the English Premier League has gradually displaced traditional working-class supporters. What this commodification of athletic talent risks producing is a sport tilted toward shareholders rather than communities.

Equally important, however, is the evidence that sport's cultural function persists. Fan-engagement studies, including longitudinal work on European football supporters, suggest that emotional identification with clubs has, if anything, intensified in the digital age. Mega-events such as the Olympics and World Cup continue to forge national camaraderie and to elevate underdog narratives — Leicester City's 2016 Premier League title remains a case in point — that no purely commercial product can manufacture on demand. However lucrative elite competition has become, it still functions as a vehicle for collective identity and aspirational role models.

My own view is that commercialisation has transformed sport's cultural value rather than annihilated it. Were broadcasting revenue more equitably redistributed toward grassroots facilities, the inspirational and integrative functions of sport could be substantially reinforced. The problem, in other words, is not commerce itself but governance failure.

To conclude, I partly agree with the commercialisation critique, yet I reject its strongest form. Elite sport retains profound cultural value; what it requires is reform of its institutions, not a romanticised retreat to a pre-commercial past.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. The two teams show real camaraderie, always supporting each other on and off the pitch. --- CAMARADERIE (n) = tình đồng đội, sự gắn kết; collocation "a spirit of camaraderie", "genuine camaraderie"; chú ý chính tả, không phải "comraderie".

2. She showed remarkable tenacity, refusing to give up even after losing the first two sets. --- TENACITY (n) = sự kiên trì, bền bỉ; collocation "sheer/mental tenacity", "show great tenacity"; không nhầm với "tension".
3. Nobody expected the underdog to win the league, but the newly promoted club did. --- UNDERDOG (n) = kẻ yếu thế, bị đánh giá thấp; luôn là danh từ, không dùng như tính từ mô tả trận đấu.
4. The defending champion was a formidable opponent in the final. --- FORMIDABLE (adj) = đáng gờm; collocation "a formidable opponent/team"; trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết đầu.
5. Signing with a major club can be an extremely lucrative move for a young player. --- LUCRATIVE (adj) = sinh lời; collocation "a lucrative deal/contract"; không nhầm với "luxurious".
6. Professional gamers need immense agility, both physical and mental, to compete at the top level. --- AGILITY (n) = sự nhanh nhẹn, linh hoạt; danh từ không đếm được; tính từ tương ứng là "agile".

The sporting achievement I find most quietly extraordinary is Eliud Kipchoge's INEOS 1:59 marathon — the moment in October 2019 when he ran 42.195 kilometres in under two hours, on a closed circuit in Vienna. It wasn't an official world-record attempt, but as a feat of human possibility, it remains, for me, almost without parallel.

What makes this particular achievement so compelling is that it was as much a scientific project as an athletic one. The two-hour barrier had been the marathon's equivalent of the four-minute mile — long held to be physiologically out of reach. Joyner's landmark 2017 paper in the Journal of Applied Physiology had predicted a theoretical limit of 1:57:58, but most exercise physiologists doubted it would be touched in our lifetimes. Kipchoge's team drew on cutting-edge research in VO₂-max periodisation, lactate-threshold management, and aerodynamic drafting; the pacing rotation alone was modelled with the precision of a flight plan.

What I find most striking, though, isn't the technology — it's Kipchoge's psychological architecture. His mantra, "no human is limited", isn't bravado; it's a remarkably disciplined cognitive frame. In post-race interviews he spoke not of pain but of trust — trust in the training, the team, the process. That, to me, is the lesson worth absorbing.

Personally, the run has reshaped how I approach my own modest 10K training. I've started structuring blocks around proper periodisation rather than ad-hoc effort, and the results, even at my amateur level, have been measurable. Were I to distil what Kipchoge teaches, it's this: tenacity is a system, not a sentiment — and the ceiling is almost always lower than reality.

Lecture title: "The Mental Edge: Sports Psychology, Overtraining and the Cost of Elite Performance"
1. Section Type

2. Pre-Listening Vocabulary (4–5 words)

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas
The lecturer will argue mental factors decide elite outcomes as much as physical talent.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Welcome back. In our final lecture on elite performance, I want to debunk the romantic myth that champions are forged through sheer physical relentlessness. The evidence — neuroscientific, longitudinal, occasionally tragic — tells a more subtle story.

> Consider this: among Olympic-level athletes within five percent of one another physiologically, what separates gold from twelfth place is overwhelmingly psychological. That's the domain of sports psychology, and its findings are now non-negotiable in elite coaching.

> Three constructs matter most. First, mental tenacity — the capacity to reframe a missed penalty or a torn ligament as actionable feedback rather than catastrophe. Second, arousal regulation — neither too anxious nor too complacent; performance peaks in what Yerkes and Dodson called the inverted-U. Third, visualisation: rehearsing motor sequences in the mind's eye, which fMRI studies show activates the very same neural pathways as physical practice.

> Now, the dark side. Overtraining syndrome — sometimes labelled non-functional overreaching — is rampant in endurance sport. Athletes who push past recovery thresholds present with elevated resting heart rate, chronic fatigue, mood disturbance and, paradoxically, a measurable drop in performance. The cure is counterintuitive: rest. Periodisation — the structured alternation of stress and recovery — is no longer optional; it is the bedrock of modern training science.

> One sobering data point: a 2021 meta-analysis estimated that up to sixty percent of distance runners experience symptoms of overtraining at least once per competitive season. That's not weakness; that's a system error in how we conceptualise effort.

Now, that Tour de France case will land better if I first add a layer the periodisation story tends to gloss over — the question of who, exactly, gets to rest. Because here's an uncomfortable wrinkle in the science. The recovery prescription assumes an athlete with the autonomy to back off. But in professional cycling, in gymnastics, in any sport with a thin contract and a queue of replacements behind you, easing off the training load can feel like signing your own redundancy. [pause] So overtraining syndrome isn't purely a physiological miscalculation; it's frequently a rational response to a brutal incentive structure. Tell a domestique to rest and you may, um, be telling him to lose his place on the team.

Let me also introduce a construct we haven't named yet but which sits right at the heart of elite psychology: self-determination theory, developed by Deci and Ryan. Their longitudinal work suggests that athletes whose motivation is intrinsic — driven by mastery and the intrinsic joy of the craft — show markedly more durable performance and lower burnout than those driven extrinsically by medals, sponsorship or parental pressure. Well, that finding cuts against the macho coaching folklore that fear and external pressure forge champions. The data say the opposite: the externally pressured athlete is the one who fractures first under load.

And there's a sharper edge still — the safeguarding dimension. The 2021 USA Gymnastics revelations, and similar reckonings in swimming and athletics, exposed how a culture fixated on relentlessness can shade into outright abuse, with young athletes coerced past every protective threshold their bodies signalled. [pause] So the mental edge I've described isn't only a route to gold; properly understood, it's also a duty of care. Which raises the obvious question of how governing bodies, federations and funding agencies ought to redesign the very environment in which athletes train — and that institutional question is precisely where I want to steer us as we close…

> The take-home message is unambiguous. The mental edge is not an ornament on top of physical preparation — it is the preparation. Coaches who ignore this, frankly, are coaching the last century's sport. Right, before we close, one quick case study from the Tour de France…

•  Overview — two opposing trends: traditional sports declined while emerging activities rose; the lines converge by 2020 (no figures).

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~179 từ)
The line graph compares participation rates in four sports — football, swimming, cycling and yoga — among UK adults over a thirty-year span from 1990 to 2020.

Overall, two contrasting trends are evident: traditional sports such as football and swimming experienced a steady decline, whereas cycling and especially yoga witnessed sustained growth. By the end of the period, the historically dominant activities had been overtaken by these newer pursuits, and all four lines converged within a narrow band.

In 1990, swimming was by far the most popular activity at 22%, followed by football at 14%; cycling and yoga remained marginal, at 6% and just 1% respectively. Over the following decades, swimming and football slipped to 11% and 10% by 2020, with football briefly peaking at 16% in 2000 before falling away.

Conversely, cycling rose steadily from 6% to 15%, overtaking football around 2010. Yoga underwent the most dramatic expansion of all, climbing fourteenfold to finish level with cycling at 14%. As a result, by the end of the period the four sports were separated by only five percentage points.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~173 từ)
The line graph traces participation rates in four sports — football, swimming, cycling and yoga — among UK adults at decade intervals between 1990 and 2020.

Overall, a clear reversal of fortunes is apparent: the once-dominant traditional sports drifted downwards, while the formerly marginal activities climbed sharply, so that the four lines converged by the close of the period. What had begun as a wide spread of popularity ended in near parity.

In 1990, swimming led comfortably at 22%, with football a distant second at 14%, whereas cycling and yoga languished at 6% and a mere 1%. Thereafter both established sports lost ground: swimming contracted year on year to 11%, while football, having peaked at 16% in 2000, slipped to 10% by 2020.

The emerging pursuits told the opposite story. Cycling advanced steadily upwards to reach 15%, overtaking football at around 2010, while yoga surged fourteenfold to 14%. Strikingly, yoga's gain of thirteen percentage points almost exactly mirrored swimming's loss of eleven, as though one sport's following had migrated wholesale to the other.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  Band 8 mở overview bằng hình ảnh tổng hợp ('a clear reversal of fortunes', 'wide spread… ended in near parity') thay vì chỉ liệt kê hai xu hướng như Band 7.
•  Band 8 dùng lexis hiếm và nominalisation dày hơn ('languished', 'contracted year on year', 'migrated wholesale') cùng phân từ 'having peaked', nâng Lexical Resource và Grammatical Range.
•  Band 8 chốt bằng nhận xét đối xứng tinh tế (yoga +13pp ≈ swimming −11pp) — quan sát 'mirror-image' đặc trưng band 7.5+, trong khi Band 7 chỉ nêu khoảng cách năm điểm.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)
•  Quét cực trị trước (30s): điểm xuất phát cao nhất (swimming 22%), điểm kết cao nhất (cycling 15%), môn biến động mạnh nhất (yoga 1→14). Khóa vào Overview.
•  Ghép cặp các đường (30s): bốn đường = hai cặp — nhóm giảm (football, swimming) và nhóm tăng (cycling, yoga). Tuyệt đối không mô tả bốn đường rời rạc.
•  Xác định điểm giao cắt (crossover): quanh 2010 cycling vượt football — đây là 'mỏ vàng' cho câu so sánh band 7+.
•  Sắp xếp thân bài theo cặp, không theo từng môn: đoạn 2 nhóm giảm, đoạn 3 nhóm tăng + nhận xét hội tụ.
•  Định lượng đa dạng: percentage points (pp) cho thay đổi cộng, bội số ('fourteenfold') cho thay đổi tỷ lệ, 'nearly halved' cho biến thể; tránh 'went up and down' (dùng fluctuated/plateaued/peaked).

Phía đồng ý (thương mại hoá đã bào mòn giá trị):
•  Bản quyền phát sóng và tài trợ đẩy giá vé tăng vọt, gạt người hâm mộ bình dân khỏi sân (vd: Premier League).

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~287 words)

It is often claimed that the relentless commercialisation of elite professional sport has stripped it of its cultural meaning. While I partly accept this argument, I believe the cultural core of sport remains largely intact.

Those who agree with the commercialisation critique tend to focus on the influence of money at the top level. What now drives many leagues is broadcasting revenue rather than community loyalty: ticket prices in the English Premier League, for example, have risen sharply, pricing ordinary supporters out of stadiums. Governance scandals at FIFA and the IOC have further damaged public trust, and sponsorship contracts sometimes appear to outweigh sporting integrity. From this perspective, sport looks increasingly like an entertainment commodity.

On the other hand, however lucrative modern sport has become, it continues to inspire fans in ways few other cultural products can. Major tournaments routinely unite entire nations behind a shared narrative, and underdog stories — a small club overcoming a far stronger opponent, as Leicester City did in 2016 — still produce moments of genuine camaraderie. Fan-engagement studies suggest that emotional attachment to clubs is deepening rather than weakening in the digital era, which implies that cultural value has been reshaped rather than erased.

In my view, the truth lies between the two positions. Commercialisation has undeniably distorted parts of elite sport, particularly competitive balance and accessibility, but its communal and aspirational dimensions endure. If broadcasting revenue were redistributed more fairly to grassroots clubs, the cultural value of sport could in fact be reinforced rather than diminished.

To conclude, I partly agree that commercialisation has eroded certain traditional aspects of elite sport, yet I do not believe its cultural significance has been lost. Better governance, not nostalgia, is the appropriate response.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~302 words)

Few claims provoke as much debate among sports commentators as the charge that elite professional sport has, through relentless commercialisation, lost its cultural value. While the critique captures real distortions, I only partly agree: the financialisation of sport has reshaped, rather than dismantled, its cultural significance.

There is, admittedly, considerable substance to the commercialisation critique. So heavily are top leagues now dependent on broadcasting rights and corporate sponsorship that the locus of decision-making has shifted from clubs to media conglomerates. Governance scandals at FIFA and the IOC have eroded public trust, while ticket-price inflation in competitions such as the English Premier League has gradually displaced traditional working-class supporters. What this commodification of athletic talent risks producing is a sport tilted toward shareholders rather than communities.

Equally important, however, is the evidence that sport's cultural function persists. Fan-engagement studies, including longitudinal work on European football supporters, suggest that emotional identification with clubs has, if anything, intensified in the digital age. Mega-events such as the Olympics and World Cup continue to forge national camaraderie and to elevate underdog narratives — Leicester City's 2016 Premier League title remains a case in point — that no purely commercial product can manufacture on demand. However lucrative elite competition has become, it still functions as a vehicle for collective identity and aspirational role models.

My own view is that commercialisation has transformed sport's cultural value rather than annihilated it. Were broadcasting revenue more equitably redistributed toward grassroots facilities, the inspirational and integrative functions of sport could be substantially reinforced. The problem, in other words, is not commerce itself but governance failure.

To conclude, I partly agree with the commercialisation critique, yet I reject its strongest form. Elite sport retains profound cultural value; what it requires is reform of its institutions, not a romanticised retreat to a pre-commercial past.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 triển khai cấu trúc cao cấp xuyên suốt (inversion 'So heavily are top leagues… dependent', cleft 'What this commodification… risks producing is', đảo ngữ điều kiện 'Were broadcasting revenue redistributed') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng vài lần.

•  Band 8 dẫn bằng chứng cụ thể hơn ('longitudinal work on European football supporters', 'media conglomerates') và nominalisation dày ('the financialisation of sport', 'the locus of decision-making'), nâng Task Response và Lexical Resource.

•  Band 8 dùng connector tinh tế ('There is, admittedly', 'Equally important, however', 'in other words') và register học thuật nhất quán, không còn cụm hơi đời thường như 'looks increasingly like' của bản 7.

vocabulary.common_error: 'Grassroots' luôn viết liền, không có dấu gạch nối; dùng như tính từ đứng trước danh từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to the most basic level of an activity or organisation, especially at community or beginner level
vocabulary.definition_vi: ở cấp cơ sở, phong trào quần chúng
vocabulary.example: Governments must invest heavily in grassroots sports facilities, making them accessible to youth from all socioeconomic backgrounds.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'grass' (cỏ) + 'roots' (rễ) → rễ cỏ, tận gốc → cấp cơ sở, khởi đầu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự kiên trì, nỗ lực bền bỉ để đạt được mục tiêu dù gặp khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It was sheer **perseverance**, more than raw talent, that carried her through years of setbacks to an Olympic medal.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'per-' (xuyên suốt) + 'severe' (khắc nghiệt) → kiên trì vượt qua điều kiện khắc nghiệt.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'perseverance' (kiên trì) với 'preservation' (bảo tồn) — hai từ dễ đọc/viết lẫn.
vocabulary.definition_en: continued effort to achieve something despite difficulties, failure, or opposition
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự kiên trì, nỗ lực bền bỉ
vocabulary.example: It was sheer perseverance, more than raw talent, that carried her through years of setbacks to an Olympic medal.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'per-' (xuyên suốt) + 'severe' (khắc nghiệt) → kiên trì vượt qua điều kiện khắc nghiệt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Việc sử dụng chất cấm để tăng cường thành tích thi đấu một cách bất hợp pháp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The athlete lost several sponsorship deals after a **doping** scandal was exposed.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'dope' (chất kích thích) + -ing → hành vi sử dụng chất kích thích để gian lận.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Doping' không đếm được; muốn nói về một vụ việc cụ thể phải dùng 'a doping scandal/case', không nói 'a doping'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the use of banned substances to illegally enhance athletic performance
vocabulary.definition_vi: việc sử dụng chất cấm để tăng thành tích
vocabulary.example: The athlete lost several sponsorship deals after a doping scandal was exposed.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'dope' (chất kích thích) + -ing → hành vi sử dụng chất kích thích để gian lận.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nghịch cảnh, hoàn cảnh khó khăn cần phải vượt qua.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Overcoming **adversity** is often what separates champions from merely talented athletes.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'adverse' (bất lợi) + -ity → adversity → hoàn cảnh bất lợi, nghịch cảnh.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'adversity' (nghịch cảnh) với 'diversity' (sự đa dạng) — âm gần giống nhưng nghĩa hoàn toàn khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: a difficult or unfavourable situation, especially one involving hardship or setbacks
vocabulary.definition_vi: nghịch cảnh, khó khăn
vocabulary.example: Overcoming adversity is often what separates champions from merely talented athletes.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'adverse' (bất lợi) + -ity → adversity → hoàn cảnh bất lợi, nghịch cảnh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự tài trợ tài chính hoặc vật chất, thường đổi lại bằng quảng cáo.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Commanding lucrative **sponsorships** now rivals prize money as the main source of income for top athletes.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sponsor' (nhà tài trợ) + -ship (trạng thái, mối quan hệ) → sponsorship → sự tài trợ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Sponsorship' là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ hành động/mối quan hệ tài trợ; 'sponsor' mới là người/tổ chức tài trợ.
vocabulary.definition_en: financial or material support given to a person or event, typically in exchange for advertising or publicity
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự tài trợ
vocabulary.example: Commanding lucrative sponsorships now rivals prize money as the main source of income for top athletes.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sponsor' (nhà tài trợ) + -ship (trạng thái, mối quan hệ) → sponsorship → sự tài trợ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự thương mại hoá một hoạt động vốn không mang tính kinh doanh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Astronomical wages shift the focus from pure sportsmanship and passion to blatant **commercialisation**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'commerce' (thương mại) + -ialisation → biến điều gì thành hoạt động thương mại.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh dùng '-isation' (commercialisation), không phải '-ization' như tiếng Anh-Mỹ.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of managing or running something, chiefly with the intention of making a profit
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự thương mại hoá
vocabulary.example: Astronomical wages shift the focus from pure sportsmanship and passion to blatant commercialisation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'commerce' (thương mại) + -ialisation → biến điều gì thành hoạt động thương mại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự bền bỉ, khả năng phục hồi nhanh sau khó khăn hoặc thất bại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The team showed remarkable **resilience** to come back from a 2-0 deficit and win the final.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
're-' (lại) + 'silire' (nhảy, gốc Latin) → nảy lại sau cú ngã → khả năng phục hồi.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Resilience' là danh từ, tính từ là 'resilient'; đừng dùng 'resilience' để bổ nghĩa cho danh từ khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: the capacity to recover quickly from difficulties; mental toughness under pressure
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự bền bỉ, khả năng phục hồi tinh thần
vocabulary.example: The team showed remarkable resilience to come back from a 2-0 deficit and win the final.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 're-' (lại) + 'silire' (nhảy, gốc Latin) → nảy lại sau cú ngã → khả năng phục hồi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình trạng tập luyện quá sức, không có đủ thời gian phục hồi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Non-functional overreaching can progress into full **overtraining** syndrome if athletes ignore their recovery thresholds.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'over' (quá) + 'training' (tập luyện) → tập luyện vượt ngưỡng phục hồi của cơ thể.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'overtraining' (hội chứng do tập quá sức kéo dài) với 'overreaching' (giai đoạn ngắn hạn, có thể hồi phục).
vocabulary.definition_en: training excessively without adequate recovery, leading to chronic fatigue and declining performance
vocabulary.definition_vi: tập luyện quá sức
vocabulary.example: Non-functional overreaching can progress into full overtraining syndrome if athletes ignore their recovery thresholds.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'over' (quá) + 'training' (tập luyện) → tập luyện vượt ngưỡng phục hồi của cơ thể.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự phân kỳ tập luyện thể thao thành các chu kỳ khoa học để tối ưu hiệu suất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I've started structuring my training blocks around proper **periodisation** rather than ad-hoc effort.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'period' (chu kỳ) + -isation → chia quá trình tập luyện thành các chu kỳ có kế hoạch.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh dùng '-isation'; đây là thuật ngữ chuyên ngành khoa học thể thao, không dùng trong văn nói thông thường.
vocabulary.definition_en: the systematic planning of athletic training in cycles to optimise performance and recovery
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự phân kỳ tập luyện (theo chu kỳ khoa học)
vocabulary.example: I've started structuring my training blocks around proper periodisation rather than ad-hoc effort.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'period' (chu kỳ) + -isation → chia quá trình tập luyện thành các chu kỳ có kế hoạch.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bỏ cuộc, đầu hàng, không tiếp tục cố gắng nữa.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The grueling training was so exhausting that I almost **threw in the towel**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Xuất xứ từ quyền anh: huấn luyện viên ném khăn vào sàn đấu để xin dừng trận → đầu hàng.
collocations: refuse to throw in the towel
ready to throw in the towel
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom cố định, không đổi 'towel' thành số nhiều hay thêm tính từ ở giữa cụm.
vocabulary.definition_en: to give up or admit defeat, especially after a difficult struggle
vocabulary.definition_vi: bỏ cuộc, đầu hàng
vocabulary.example: The grueling training was so exhausting that I almost threw in the towel.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Xuất xứ từ quyền anh: huấn luyện viên ném khăn vào sàn đấu để xin dừng trận → đầu hàng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sân chơi công bằng, nơi mọi người đều có cơ hội ngang nhau.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Strict anti-doping rules are essential to ensure a **level playing field** for all competitors.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Sân bóng phẳng, không nghiêng bên nào → cơ hội thi đấu công bằng cho cả hai đội.
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm cố định 'a level playing field', không dùng số nhiều 'fields' dù nói về nhiều lĩnh vực.
vocabulary.definition_en: a situation in which everyone has an equal chance of succeeding, with no unfair advantages
vocabulary.definition_vi: sân chơi công bằng
vocabulary.example: Strict anti-doping rules are essential to ensure a level playing field for all competitors.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Sân bóng phẳng, không nghiêng bên nào → cơ hội thi đấu công bằng cho cả hai đội.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hành động quá vội vàng, làm điều gì trước khi đúng thời điểm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Don't **jump the gun** and start celebrating before the referee blows the final whistle.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Xuất xứ điền kinh: vận động viên xuất phát trước tiếng súng lệnh → hành động quá sớm.
collocations: jumped the gun by doing sth
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom không chia số nhiều; luôn giữ nguyên dạng 'jump/jumped the gun'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to act before the appropriate or agreed time; to start something too soon
vocabulary.definition_vi: hành động vội vàng, làm trước khi đến lúc
vocabulary.example: Don't jump the gun and start celebrating before the referee blows the final whistle.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Xuất xứ điền kinh: vận động viên xuất phát trước tiếng súng lệnh → hành động quá sớm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Là người ra quyết định quan trọng, nắm quyền chỉ đạo.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> In this team, the captain is the one who **calls the shots** on the field.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'shots' như những cú đánh trong thể thao → người 'gọi' từng cú đánh là người chỉ đạo cuộc chơi.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng số nhiều 'shots', không nói 'call the shot'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be the person who makes the important decisions; to be in control
vocabulary.definition_vi: người ra quyết định, nắm quyền chỉ đạo
vocabulary.example: In this team, the captain is the one who calls the shots on the field.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'shots' như những cú đánh trong thể thao → người 'gọi' từng cú đánh là người chỉ đạo cuộc chơi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thay đổi luật chơi hoặc mục tiêu một cách bất công giữa chừng, khiến việc thành công khó hơn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It's incredibly frustrating to succeed when the management keeps **moving the goalposts**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tưởng tượng khung thành bị dịch chuyển giữa trận đấu → không thể ghi bàn dù đã cố gắng đúng hướng.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng số nhiều 'goalposts'; nói về hành vi thay đổi tiêu chí, không phải vật thể thật trên sân.
vocabulary.definition_en: to unfairly change the rules or targets of a situation partway through, making it harder to succeed
vocabulary.definition_vi: thay đổi luật chơi/mục tiêu một cách bất công giữa chừng
vocabulary.example: It's incredibly frustrating to succeed when the management keeps moving the goalposts.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tưởng tượng khung thành bị dịch chuyển giữa trận đấu → không thể ghi bàn dù đã cố gắng đúng hướng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Một cách dễ dàng, rõ ràng không cần bàn cãi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> With their newly acquired star player, they should easily win the match **hands down**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Xuất xứ đua ngựa: kỵ sĩ thắng dễ đến mức buông tay cương (hands down) mà vẫn về nhất.
vocabulary.common_error: Đứng cuối câu, sau động từ chính; không dùng như tính từ đứng trước danh từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: easily and without question; clearly the best or the winner
vocabulary.definition_vi: một cách dễ dàng, không cần bàn cãi
vocabulary.example: With their newly acquired star player, they should easily win the match hands down.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Xuất xứ đua ngựa: kỵ sĩ thắng dễ đến mức buông tay cương (hands down) mà vẫn về nhất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Lợi thế có được ngay từ lúc bắt đầu một cuộc thi hoặc hoạt động.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Taking private tennis lessons at a young age gave him a massive **head start** over the other beginners.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'head' (đầu) + 'start' (bắt đầu) → bắt đầu trước, dẫn đầu ngay từ đầu.
vocabulary.common_error: Đi với giới từ 'over sb', không phải 'to sb'; là danh từ ghép, thường viết rời hoặc có gạch nối.
vocabulary.definition_en: an advantage given or gained at the beginning of a competition or activity
vocabulary.definition_vi: lợi thế khởi đầu
vocabulary.example: Taking private tennis lessons at a young age gave him a massive head start over the other beginners.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'head' (đầu) + 'start' (bắt đầu) → bắt đầu trước, dẫn đầu ngay từ đầu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chất kích thích bị cấm mà vận động viên sử dụng để tăng thành tích một cách gian lận.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The Olympic committee strictly bans any athlete caught taking **performance-enhancing drugs**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'performance' (thành tích) + 'enhancing' (tăng cường) + 'drugs' (chất) → chất giúp tăng thành tích bất hợp pháp.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường viết tắt là 'PEDs'; cụm này luôn ở dạng danh từ ghép, không tách rời 'performance' và 'enhancing'.
vocabulary.definition_en: substances used illegally by athletes to artificially improve physical performance
vocabulary.definition_vi: chất kích thích tăng cường thành tích (bị cấm)
vocabulary.example: The Olympic committee strictly bans any athlete caught taking performance-enhancing drugs.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'performance' (thành tích) + 'enhancing' (tăng cường) + 'drugs' (chất) → chất giúp tăng thành tích bất hợp pháp.
